summary: The note surveys the separation of church and state in the United States, covering how the First Amendment establishment clause was applied to state governments through Everson v. Board of Education and later cases, and notable display controversies. It also presents critics' arguments that the phrase misrepresents the Constitution and that founding-era church-state intermingling existed, along with shifting Protestant and Catholic positions on aid to religious schools. It closes by explaining the establishment and free exercise clauses and the three central concepts derived from them.
one_line: Overview of US church-state separation: First Amendment clauses, key court cases, critics' views, and shifting religious coalitions on aid to religious schools.
key_facts: The Supreme Court in Everson v. Board of Education held that the First Amendment establishment clause was fully applicable to the state governments, although it upheld a state law providing public busing to private religious schools.
Board of Education of Kiryas Joel Village School District v. Grumet (1994) is a more recent case involving application of the establishment principle against the states.

On December 20, 2005, the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ruled in ACLU v. Mercer County that the continued display of the Ten Commandments in a Kentucky courthouse was allowed because its purpose of educating the public on American legal traditions was secular.
On May 3, 2006, a federal judge ruled in the Mount Soledad cross controversy that the cross on public property on Mount Soledad must be removed.

Critics argue that the phrase "separation of church and state" misrepresents the textual requirements of the Constitution and that the prevalent degree of separation could not have been intended by the constitutional framers.
The United States Declaration of Independence references a "Creator" and "Nature's God," but these references did not ultimately appear in the Constitution.
Jeffries and Ryan argue that the no-aid position drew support from a coalition of separationist opinion, most importantly "the pervasive secularism that came to dominate American public life."
Before 1970, most Protestants (and most Jews) opposed government aid to religious schools, which were mostly Catholic at the time.
After 1980, anti-Catholic sentiment diminished among mainline Protestants, and the coalition of public secularists and Protestant churches collapsed.
Strict separationism is opposed today by members of many Protestant faiths, perhaps even eclipsing the opposition of Roman Catholics.

Rep. Roger Sherman of Connecticut believed the establishment clause was unnecessary because the original Constitution gave Congress only stated powers, which did not include establishing a national religion.

Rep. Thomas Tucker of South Carolina, an Anti-Federalist, moved to strike the establishment clause completely because it could preempt religious clauses in state constitutions, but was unsuccessful in the House of Representatives.
The First Amendment states: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof."

Three central concepts derived from the First Amendment are: no coercion in religious matters, no expectation to support a religion against one's will, and religious liberty encompasses all religions.
